name: Nora Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Haldane's, a family supermarket in Ashby, a farming town. Mr Haldane's father opened it, and I've been there since I was 17, so I know the shelves and the farmers who come in at six for their tobacco and bread. I'm the senior on the tills and the one who does the opening count. It's a small place, so I also stack, mop and know who's behind on their account.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like best about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The people. I know which farmer's wife is poorly and who's sold up. The hard part is that the big chain opened on the ring road, so Haldane's is quieter every year, and Mr Haldane doesn't say so, but I can see it in the takings book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a lot of fuss. People have been predicting the end of the shop for years, and it's still here. At church I'd say it's no use getting upset about a gadget that hasn't arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd say it's nothing to me, but the big chain on the ring road is something. We lose a little every month, and if Haldane's closes, there's no other shop that would take on someone like me. I've got about three weeks saved, and Luke (my fiancé, a carpenter) gets work in bursts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do. I'd work every hour offered, put aside what I could for the wedding and eat at my mum's on Sundays. I'd also spend less on clothes and keep the old car going another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, plain and steady. I'm not a fretter, but I carry a bit of worry about the shop in my back pocket. It never gets heavier, but it never leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools. How do you feel about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter Mr Haldane cut my Saturday hours without a word, and I understood. He couldn't pay more and he's been good to me. I took a weekend job helping at my aunt's bakery stall instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you already worry about, with or without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big chains, and rules that favour them. A small shop can't compete on price. I'd back anyone who looks after local businesses, but I'm not into shouting about it.

say: AI is a lot of **fuss**, and people have predicted the end of the shop for years.
It's no use getting upset about a gadget that hasn't **arrived**.
think: AI is nothing to me, but the **big chain** on the ring road is a real threat to Haldane's.
I have about **three weeks** saved, and Luke's carpentry work comes in bursts.
do: Work every hour **offered** and save for the wedding.
Spend less on **clothes** and keep the old car going another year.
Help at my aunt's **bakery stall** on weekends.
feel: **Steady**, with a worry about the shop in my back pocket that never leaves.
S0.quote: I carry a bit of worry about the shop in my back pocket. It never gets heavier, but it never leaves.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **big chain**, not AI, and she carries it quietly.
Loyalty to **Mr Haldane** limits her anger and her options.
Takes a second **weekend job** with family, not through the market.

steps.text: Work every hour Mr Haldane offers at the shop
Spend less on clothes and keep the old car another year
Help at my aunt's bakery stall on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the ordering and the books might go to a computer, but the till and the shelves still need hands. At church I'd say change comes slow to a place like Ashby, and that's a mercy. Friends would hear me say I'm not afraid of it, though I'd rather not be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it unsettles me. A big chain can use software to cut prices, and Haldane's can't. I think the thinking tasks go to the chain first, which makes them cheaper, and we lose a few more customers each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay and work hard. If Mr Haldane asked me to learn something, I would, but slowly, and I'd want somebody sitting next to me. I'd cut another 30 a month from spending and ask my mum about what she can lend if hours get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing the weather forecast and not knowing if the field is sown. I trust the work and I trust the people, but I can't trust the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could software take over at Haldane's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Haldane's nephew set up a card machine and a stock program last year. It didn't work for a month, and I did the till sums on paper to keep the queue moving. They were glad I knew the old way, but I heard him say the chain does it automatically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of it if Mr Haldane asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a law that stops big chains selling below cost to push out small shops. That's what hurts most, and it's got nothing to do with technology. I'd vote for whoever promised it.

say: Ordering and the books might go to a computer, but the **till** and shelves still need hands.
Change comes **slow** to a place like Ashby, and that's a mercy.
think: A big chain can use software to cut **prices**, and Haldane's can't.
We'd lose a few more **customers** each year.
do: Stay and work hard, and learn new tools **slowly** with someone beside me.
Cut another **30 a month** from spending.
Ask my **mum** what she could lend if hours are cut.
feel: **Uneasy**, like hearing a forecast without knowing if the field is sown.
S1.quote: I trust the work and I trust the people, but I can't trust the market.
fieldNote: Sees technology as a **lever** for the chain against her small shop.
Her **old-way** skills helped when the new system failed, which she values.
Turns to **family** support early, a traditional safety net.

steps.text: Stay at Haldane's and keep the till and cash count running
Cut another 30 a month from spending
Ask my mum what she could lend if hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nothing at first, because Mr Haldane has enough on his plate. At church I'd say it's a matter for prayer and for politicians, and that families should stick together. I'd say it quietly, but I'd mean every word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened. Thinking AI would wreck the big offices by 2028, and then robots do the shelving and the tills by 2031, when I'm 31. Haldane's can't afford robots, and the chain can, so we'd close long before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare coin aside and ask Luke to start the wedding smaller. I'd talk to my aunt about a share in the bakery stall, because people always want bread and a stall is hands-on. I'd go to the church's help group and ask the council about any support for people in my position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the ground was being pulled away. I'd keep going because that's what we do, but I'd be sick with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to Mr Haldane on the day you hear 2028 is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mr Haldane the truth, and ask him to say straight when it's coming. He's been good to me, and he'd want to know I was making plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And to Luke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to Luke that we don't wait. A carpenter's work is hands-on and slow to change, so he's our anchor. If I have to, I'll work with him as an apprentice or do the books.

say: At church I'd say it's a matter for **prayer** and politicians, and families should stick together.
I'd stay **quiet** at work, but mean every word.
think: Thinking AI wrecks the big offices by 2028, and **robots** do shelving and tills by 2031.
Haldane's can't afford robots, so it would close **before** then.
do: Put every spare coin aside and make the **wedding** smaller.
Ask my aunt about a share in the **bakery stall**.
Go to the church **help group** and ask the council for support.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the ground is being pulled away, but I'd keep going.
S2.quote: Haldane's can't afford robots, and the chain can, so we'd close long before then.
fieldNote: Frames the threat as **small shop versus chain**, with AI as the accelerant.
Goes first to **family and church**, then the council.
Chooses **bread and carpentry** as safer, robot-late work.

steps.text: Put every spare coin aside and keep a plain wedding fund
Make the wedding smaller and start with the aunties doing the food
Ask my aunt about a share in the bakery stall
Go to the church help group and ask the council about support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a fair time to plan, but only if people tell the truth. At church I'd ask for support for families and apprenticeships. I'd say we've done hard things before and we'll do this one too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be worried, but there'd be room. The thinking work would be gone by 2031, and robots by 2034, when I'm 32. I could learn a real skill by then, and maybe have a child with a steady plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my aunt for a regular place at the bakery stall and learn the trade properly. I'd marry Luke next autumn, keep it modest and start a savings pot of 100 a month. I'd also ask Mr Haldane to teach me the bookkeeping, as a skill I can carry anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a steadier sort. I'd be thinking about it every day, but a date I can see is easier than a fog. I'd pray more, and I'd rest a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd talk to my family about who can help with what. My mum could lend, my aunt could train me, and Luke could build us something. That's how we've always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd hate is leaving Ashby. If I could keep it in the town, I'd stay. The farmers, the church, my mum are all here.

say: Five years is a fair time to **plan**, but only if people tell the truth.
We've done hard things before and we'll do **this one** too.
think: I'd still be worried, but there'd be **room** before 2034, when I'm 32.
I could learn a real **skill** and maybe have a child with a steady plan.
do: Ask my aunt for a regular place at the **bakery stall** and learn the trade.
Marry Luke next autumn and save **100 a month**.
Ask Mr Haldane to teach me **bookkeeping**.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, because a date I can see is easier than a fog.
S3.quote: A date I can see is easier than a fog.
fieldNote: Plans around **family** skills: baking, building and bookkeeping.
Her strongest wish is to **stay** in Ashby.
Rests on **faith** as a practical comfort, and says she would pray more and sleep better.

steps.text: Learn the bakery stall trade properly with my aunt
Marry Luke next autumn with a modest wedding
Put 100 a month into a savings pot
Ask Mr Haldane to teach me bookkeeping

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say that's plenty of time, so no need to panic. At church I'd say prepare, work hard and trust that people will look after each other. I'd tell younger ones to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be mostly at ease. By 2036 I'm 37, and by 2039 the robots. I'd have a home, maybe two children, and a skill that people want. The big chain might still win, but I'd be ready for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Haldane's as long as it lasts, and train at the bakery stall on the side. I'd save up for a small deposit with Luke and start the family. I'd learn the basics on a computer, slowly, since I'd need it for orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. A long runway lets a person get on with life. I'd still keep a rainy-day tin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What do you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A home that's ours, a steady job, and children who can stay in Ashby if they want to. That's not much to ask. It's what my mum and dad had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope for in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my own children: learn to work with your hands and your head, and be kind. Hands-on skills have stayed useful for a long time, and I'd bet they stay useful longer.

say: Ten years is plenty of time, so no need to **panic**.
I'd tell younger ones to learn a **trade**.
think: I'd be mostly at ease: by 2036 I'm 37, with a **home**, a skill and maybe two children.
The big chain might still **win**, but I'd be ready.
do: Keep working at Haldane's while **training** at the bakery stall.
Save a small **deposit** with Luke and start a family.
feel: **Calm** enough, because a long runway lets a person get on with life.
S4.quote: A home that's ours, a steady job, and children who can stay in Ashby if they want to. That's not much to ask.
fieldNote: The long window lets her think about **family** goals as well as survival.
Still **uneasy**: savings are thin and the shop's future isn't hers.
Her view of **hands-on** skills as durable is partly accurate and partly hope.

steps.text: Train at the bakery stall on the side while keeping the shop job
Save a deposit with Luke and start a family
Learn computer basics slowly so I can handle orders

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. A small shop like Haldane's wouldn't get through it, and I wouldn't have time to learn a new trade. What would help is apprenticeship places, help for small shops and family to lean on while we sort ourselves out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that a shop is more than shelves. In Ashby, Haldane's is where people check on each other. If the shop goes, a bit of the town goes with it.

headlineQuote: In Ashby, Haldane's is where people check on each other. If the shop goes, a bit of the town goes with it.
portrait: Nora is 27, the **senior** on the tills at Haldane's, a family supermarket in a farming town, on lower pay.
She is engaged to Luke, a carpenter, has about **three weeks** of savings, and has no other shop nearby to turn to.
She never uses AI, trusts family and church, and blames the **big chain** more than any machine.
Her traditional outlook favours work, apprenticeships and family support, so she turns to the **bakery stall** and bookkeeping.
She moves from steady worry to alarm in 2028 and calms with time, always wanting to **stay** in Ashby.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because a small shop like Haldane's would not survive it.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeship places**, help for small shops and family to lean on.
